title: Checkpoint: Gods and the Afterlife
objective: After this level you can explain how Egyptians prepared for life after death.
summary: From 70 days of embalming to the Opening of the Mouth, spells, amulets, shabtis and the scales, Egyptians prepared step by step for the Field of Reeds.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: how to pack for eternity.
cards.body: You’ve met the gods, the embalmers, the scales and the spells. Put them in order, and you get the journey Egyptians believed they would make after death.

cards.headline: The road to the Field of Reeds

events.label: Embalmers make the mummy, heart left inside
Opening of the Mouth: priests restore the senses
Book of the Dead spells guard against snakes and crocodiles
The heart is weighed against the feather of Maat
The Field of Reeds: a perfect Egypt

cards.headline: Last-minute packing
cards.body: Egyptians left little to chance. In the Opening of the Mouth ritual, priests used special tools to touch the mummy’s mouth and eyes so the spirit could eat, drink, breathe and see. And since paradise came with work, people packed shabtis: small figures buried to do their work in the afterlife. By the end of the New Kingdom, the ideal set was 365, one for each day of the year, plus overseers. Eternity, fully staffed.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: The myth of Osiris promised that death could be survived, and in time every Egyptian was linked with him at death. Mummification kept a body for the ka and ba to return to. Amulets were tucked into the wrappings. Spells rode along on papyrus. Then came the scales, and, for a heart as light as a feather, a better Egypt forever.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: Egyptians believed in many gods, pictured in many forms
Mummies kept a home for the ka and ba
Spells, amulets and shabtis prepared the dead
The heart was judged; the worthy reached the Field of Reeds

questions.prompt: Gods and the Afterlife recap: who waited by the scales to eat a heart that failed?
questions.explanation: Ammit, part crocodile, lion and hippopotamus, ate a heart that failed the weighing.

questions.prompt: Gods and the Afterlife recap: which organs did embalmers place in canopic jars?

options.label: The heart and the brain
options.rationale: The heart stayed in; the brain was often thrown away.

options.label: The lungs, stomach, liver and intestines
The eyes and the tongue
options.rationale: The jars held four internal organs.

options.label: Only the heart
options.rationale: The heart was usually left inside the body.

questions.explanation: Lungs, stomach, liver and intestines were embalmed separately and placed in canopic jars.

questions.prompt: Why did priests perform the Opening of the Mouth ritual on a mummy?

options.label: To remove the brain
options.rationale: That was the embalmers’ job, earlier.

options.label: So the spirit could eat, drink, breathe and see
To let the heart speak at the judgment
options.rationale: Egyptians hoped the heart would stay quiet.

options.label: To feed the temple’s god
options.rationale: This ritual was for the dead person.

questions.explanation: Touching the mouth and eyes with special tools was meant to let the spirit eat, drink, breathe and see.

questions.prompt: Gods and the Afterlife recap: what was a pilgrim doing when buying a mummified ibis at a temple?

options.label: Buying dinner
options.rationale: It was a gift, not food.

options.label: Paying a tax to the king
options.rationale: It was given to a god.

options.label: Making an offering to a god, Thoth

questions.explanation: Pilgrims bought mummified animals as offerings: ibises for Thoth, cats for Bastet, crocodiles for Sobek.

questions.prompt: Gods and the Afterlife recap: why did the myth of Osiris give every Egyptian burial its purpose?

options.label: Osiris lived on after death, and every Egyptian was linked with him at death
Osiris had built the first pyramid
options.rationale: The myth is about death and survival.

options.label: Osiris defeated Seth and banned funerals
Osiris was the god of mummified animals
options.rationale: He was ruler and judge of the dead.

questions.explanation: Osiris survived death as ruler of the underworld, and every Egyptian was linked with him at death: a promise for all.
